brief.notification_title: Quiet weekend before Apple, AMD, midterms, payrolls
brief.market_summary: No US stock, bond or oil market has traded since Friday, so these are still Friday's closing prices. On Friday the S&P 500 fell 1.82% to 7,580 and the Nasdaq fell 2.86%, the worst day for both since June. Semis (SMH) dropped 6.98% after Intel's weak guidance, while energy, staples, health care and utilities all rose. Treasuries rallied, led by the 5-year (-8bp to 4.72%), and the 10-year finished at 4.93%. January Brent settled at $113.43 and OPEC+ confirmed over the weekend that December output targets stay unchanged. Crypto is the only market that traded over the weekend: BTC is steady near $77.9K as Binance reopens withdrawals in phases after its $6.3B hack, but altcoins are still down 16-24% over the month.
brief.since_last: The last brief was written Saturday from Friday's closes, so stock, Treasury and oil prices haven't changed. What's new: (1) OPEC+ formally kept December targets unchanged for a third month. It pushed 2027 quotas to the 29 Nov full meeting, with a capacity review due by mid-November (n161, n42, n1). (2) Binance began phase one of withdrawals, BTC first, and says 90% of stolen user assets are now covered. About $2B left in the first 3 hours (n56, n90). The FBI blames North Korea (n106). (3) BTC held near $78K (+0.53%), while SOL (-1.39%) and ADA (-0.52%) kept lagging. (4) Weekend previews say a payrolls rebound could keep the Fed on a hiking path (n20, n138). (5) Iran said Hormuz could reopen two days after the US meets its terms (n85), a reminder that a deal could hit oil. Housekeeping: US clocks went back an hour, so index futures reopen Sunday 18:00 EST, which is 07:00 SGT Monday. Several headlines in the feed are old or recycled and I've ignored them: n135, n143, n146 ('BTC past $67K'), n147–n158, n163, n169 and n174. The GDPNow print shows a timestamp later than this brief was written, and the crypto snapshot timestamp also doesn't match the brief time. Treat both as approximate.

sections.summary: Friday's sell-off was a rotation out of AI rather than broad selling. The Nasdaq fell 2.86% and SMH 6.98%, while XLE (+1.91%), XLP (+1.41%), XLU (+0.67%) and XLV (+0.45%) rose, and the Russell 2000 still gained 1.29% on the week. Futures reopen Sunday evening ET into a week of major earnings and events: Apple Monday, the midterms and AMD Tuesday, payrolls Friday.
key_points: S&P 500 7,580.07 (-1.82%), 3.05% below the 6 Oct record of 7,818.93. The 200-day moving average is about 7,306 (BTIG), roughly 3.6% lower.
Nasdaq -5.3% in October, its worst month since March 2025. XLK -9.25% and SMH -15.43% over the month, while XLV +11.23%, XLP +11.32% and XLE +11.67%.
VIX only 19.42 despite the worst day since June. Investors are buying protection (n17), but there's no sign of capitulation.

Catalysts: Apple and Palantir Monday after the close, AMD Tuesday after the close, Qualcomm and Arm Wednesday after the close. Investors' focus has moved from how fast AI earnings grow to whether the AI spending pays off (n6, n32).

sections.summary: Treasuries rallied on the growth and AI scare, led by the front end: 5Y 4.72% (-8bp), 10Y 4.93% (-6bp), 30Y 5.31% (-2bp). All three are down about 30bp over the month. But the Fed held at 3.75–4.00% with two dissents in favour of a hike, September PCE ran at 3.6%, and previews say a payrolls rebound could keep hikes in play (n20). That limits how far yields can fall.
key_points: 13-week bill 3.97%. SGOV-type cash still earns about 4% with almost no duration risk.

IEF +2.75% and TLT +5.31% over the month, but the 30Y at 5.31% is still near levels described as two-decade highs (n165). Fiscal supply concerns (debt above $40T, n86) and Treasury's expanded buybacks (n176, n164) are part of the long-end story.
Credit is softening slightly: HYG -0.19% vs LQD +0.05% on Friday. Watch high-yield spreads if tech weakness spreads.
Wednesday's quarterly refunding and Friday's NFP (+63K expected, AHE 0.3%) are the two events for duration this week. I'm not adding IEF until both are out.

sections.summary: January Brent settled at $113.43 on Friday (+$2.63). The snapshot's -1.26% reflects the switch from the expiring December contract to January, not an actual fall. The expiring December contract settled at $117.64. OPEC+ held December targets for a third month, but most Gulf members are already producing well below quota because the Iran war disrupts exports, so the quotas barely matter right now. What matters is Hormuz flows and politics after the midterms.
key_points: Brent rose about 13.6% in October. WTI is at $104.12, leaving a roughly $9 Brent premium that reflects the risk to seaborne Gulf supply.
December traded about $4.21 above January, a steep backwardation: buyers are paying up for barrels now. It also gives long holders of BNO a positive roll yield.
OPEC+ meets in full on 29 Nov for 2027 quotas, with a capacity review by mid-November. The UAE, outside OPEC since May, is targeting more than 5M bpd (n170).

Two-way risk: Iran says Hormuz could reopen two days after the US meets its terms (n85), the IEA warns of a 2027 surplus if Gulf flows normalise (n173), and analysts warn of escalation after the midterms (n124).

About $2B moved off Binance in the first 3 hours of withdrawals (n90). ETH and BNB Chain withdrawals open in later phases, so the risk of more outflows isn't over. BNB (+0.98%) is holding up surprisingly well.
Sentiment indicators are at their lowest since FTX (n77). Galaxy calls the bottom (n31) while Cowen says it may not be in (n57). Extremes like this help timing but don't trigger a trade on their own.
BTC tends to move most around jobs and CPI releases (n105, n107), so Friday's payrolls matter more than the midterms for crypto.

brief.instructor_take: Nothing has traded since Friday except crypto, so today is about preparing for a week packed with binary events, not reacting to new prices. The most important fact is that Friday was a rotation, not a liquidation. The Nasdaq fell 2.86% and SMH 6.98%, yet energy, staples, health care and utilities rose, the Russell 2000 finished the week up 1.29%, and VIX only reached 19.42. The market is deciding who pays for the AI build-out. Intel guided Q4 EPS to $0.25 against $0.43 expected, and Amazon's trailing free cash flow is -$42.4B on about $220B of capex. That question gets answered by Apple on Monday and AMD on Tuesday night, not by Friday's tape. What I think the crowd underweights is that bonds are a poor hedge here. The 5-year fell 8bp on the growth scare, but September PCE is 3.6%, two Fed officials voted to hike, and payrolls are forecast to rebound to +63K. A hot jobs number could push yields up just as tech wobbles. So rather than buying duration as insurance, I'd cut risk directly by staying out of semis until AMD reports, and own sectors with their own earnings support: energy and health care. I'm not calling a bear market, since the S&P is only 3% off its record with the 200-day near 7,306, but there's no reward for being a hero before Tuesday night. Keep spare cash in SGOV at roughly 4%, let resting limit orders do the buying, and leave crypto alone until Binance's withdrawal phases are done and ETF flows turn positive.

top_ideas.title: Semis: stay out until AMD reports
top_ideas.one_liner: No semis dip-buying before AMD Tue; re-enter only above $530
top_ideas.thesis: SMH is down 15.43% in a month and 6.98% on Friday after Intel's guide-down. Apple reports Monday and AMD Tuesday night, so buying now pays for a good outcome before seeing it. Stay out, hold the cash in SGOV, and re-enter only on evidence.
top_ideas.reasoning: Start with the evidence. Intel beat Q3 EPS ($0.52 vs about $0.39) and still fell 28.6% because Q4 guidance of $0.25 came in far below $0.43, and its CFO sees PC weakness through the first half of 2027. Add Amazon's -$42.4B trailing free cash flow and Alphabet's record one-day drop, and the market is now asking whether AI spending earns a return. That question hits chipmakers twice: through lower valuation multiples and through the risk of smaller future orders. AMD's bar on Tuesday is $1.68 against $0.97 a year ago, and after Intel it will be judged on the data-centre guide, not the beat. I'm applying asymmetric event risk. If AMD is great, I pay a few percent more on Wednesday with confirmation. If it disappoints, I've sidestepped another day like Friday. I pick SMH rather than XLK because SMH is the concentrated bet on the capex cycle, while XLK also holds Apple and software. What a newer investor misses is that a big down day feels like a discount, but VIX at 19.42 says nobody has capitulated yet. I'm wrong if SMH closes above $530 after AMD and holds through Qualcomm and Arm on Wednesday night.

top_ideas.title: Health care: finish the position on a dip
top_ideas.one_liner: Keep half of XLV; rest a limit at $181–182 through pharma earnings
top_ideas.thesis: Money has moved out of AI-linked tech into health care, whose earnings don't depend on corporate capex budgets. This week Vertex, Pfizer, Amgen and Novo report and can confirm it. XLV has already run 11% in a month, so finish the position only on a pullback.
top_ideas.reasoning: Health care is up 11.23% in a month and 3.12% last week. That is defensive rotation, and it only lasts if the sector's own earnings hold up. This week tests that: Vertex Monday night ($4.36), Pfizer Tuesday morning ($0.72 vs $0.87 last year, a low bar), Amgen Tuesday night ($5.74), then Novo ($0.81 vs $1.02, the weakest setup) and CVS Wednesday. XLV closed at $184.87, above my $184 cap, so I'm not chasing. A limit at $181–182 lets an Apple- or AMD-driven sell-off give me a better entry, because good sectors get sold in bad markets. I use the ETF rather than single pharma names because Intel just showed that one guidance cut can cost 25%+ in a stock, but only a point or two in a diversified fund. What I'd watch that others may miss is Novo: a GLP-1 pricing disappointment could hit the large-cap pharma group for a day, which could be exactly the dip that fills the order. I'm wrong if XLV closes below $176 or if Pfizer, Amgen or Novo cut forward guidance. That would mean health care was just a hiding place, not a fundamental call.

top_ideas.sizing: 4–5% full position: about 2–2.5% held now, the other 2–2.5% via the limit.

top_ideas.title: Energy: hold 3/4, last quarter only near $68
top_ideas.one_liner: Hold XLE; add final quarter near $68 while Brent stays above $105
top_ideas.thesis: Gulf supply is still disrupted, OPEC+ is holding targets it can't even meet, and January Brent is $113 with steep backwardation. Producers are turning that into beats and buybacks. Hold most of the position and add the rest only on a dip, because a Hormuz deal could hit oil quickly.
top_ideas.reasoning: The core is supply. OPEC+ held December targets for a third month, but most Gulf members are producing well below quota because the Iran war disrupts exports, so the quotas don't matter right now. January Brent settled at $113.43 and the expiring December contract at $117.64. That $4 gap between consecutive months is steep backwardation, buyers paying up for barrels now, which is what a genuine shortage looks like. Earnings confirmed it on Friday: Exxon $4.23 vs about $4.10 with a $20B 2027 buyback, Chevron $5.28 vs $4.89. This week Diamondback, Marathon Petroleum ($25.74 vs $3.01 a year ago), ConocoPhillips and EOG should show the same. I prefer XLE to BNO because producers turn today's prices into buybacks and dividends, and their share prices assume oil well below spot, which cushions a fall in crude. BNO is a pure bet on the price itself. The risk is political: Iran says Hormuz could reopen two days after the US meets its terms (n85), and escalation after Tuesday's midterms is just as possible, so oil can gap either way. That's why I hold three-quarters and only add on a dip to about $68. A signed US–Iran or Hormuz deal, January Brent below $100, or an XLE close below $65.50 ends the idea.

XLV ($184.87): the half position stands, and the $181–182 limit for the second half is unfilled and still good through Wednesday. XLV is above the $184 cap, so no chasing. Keep. SMH ($522.49): keep the avoid. If you didn't exit Friday, the instruction to sell in Monday's first hour still applies, and futures reopening Sunday evening ET give you an early look at any bounce. Nothing over the weekend reduces the AMD risk. XLE ($70.02): keep three-quarters, and add the final quarter only near $68 with January Brent ($113.43) above $105. The OPEC+ hold was expected and doesn't change the case. lesson.concept: Guidance matters more than the beat
lesson.explanation: A stock's price reflects expected future earnings, so the quarter just reported matters less than what management says about the next one. A company can beat EPS and still collapse if it cuts guidance, because every analyst then lowers next year's estimate and the stock is re-priced on those lower numbers. Those estimate revisions, not the headline beat or miss, drive moves that last weeks. So when a report comes out, read the outlook before the EPS line.
lesson.todays_example: Intel beat Q3 EPS ($0.52 vs about $0.39 expected) but guided Q4 EPS to $0.25 against $0.43 consensus, and the stock fell 28.6%, its worst day since 1974. Amazon slightly missed EPS ($1.89 vs $1.96) yet closed only -1.41% after being down about 7% before the open, because AWS grew 39%. This week, for Apple ($1.98 bar) and AMD ($1.68 bar), the holiday-quarter outlook and the data-centre guide will matter more than whether they clear the estimate.
